title: Speak, Lord (1 Samuel 3)
hook: a boy wakes three times to a voice and learns to say speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth

segments.voice: Yesterday, Hannah at Shiloh, praying so hard the priest thought she was drunk. Your line was she poured out her soul. Whose raw words did you believe? Today, the boy she prayed for. Day three hundred ninety-eight.

It's the middle of the night in the sanctuary at Shiloh. The lamp of God hasn't gone out yet. An old priest, Eli, is asleep in his place; his eyes have grown so dim he can barely see. And a boy is asleep near the ark of God. That's Samuel, Hannah's son, the one she gave to the Lord. The text adds a sad note about those days: the word of the Lord was rare, and visions were few. Then, in the dark, someone calls the boy's name. Samuel jumps up and runs to the old man. Here I am. You called me. Eli rolls over: I didn't call you. Go back to sleep.
screen: `NIGHT AT SHILOH.` → `THE WORD OF THE LORD WAS RARE.` → `HERE I AM. YOU CALLED ME.`

segments.voice: It happens again. Samuel runs to Eli, Eli sends him back. Then a third time. And the text gives the reason he keeps getting it wrong: "Samuel did not yet know the Lord." He's grown up in the house of God, he serves there every day, and he doesn't recognize God's voice. That isn't a failure. He's simply young. On the third time, the old man understands. Eli, who has his own failings, and whose sons have been a disgrace, still knows this much: it's God. So he gives the boy one line to say. In the Douay-Rheims: "Speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth." Samuel goes back and lies down. And the text says the Lord came and stood, and called as before: Samuel, Samuel. And this time the boy says it. Notice what the line does. Speak comes first: Samuel asks for the word. Then heareth: he promises to listen. In Hebrew, heareth is the same verb as the Shema's hear, the hear, O Israel this path met not long ago. Listening is the heart of it. And what God says is hard: judgment on Eli's house. In the morning Samuel is afraid to tell him. Eli insists, and Samuel tells him everything. Hearing God, it turns out, can mean carrying a message you'd rather not. The Church reads this chapter at Sunday Mass beside the call of Jesus's first disciples in John's Gospel. And some Catholics pray speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth as a whole prayer, with no other words.
screen: `THREE TIMES TO THE WRONG ROOM.` · `SAMUEL DID NOT YET KNOW THE LORD.` · `THE OLD PRIEST GIVES HIM A LINE.` · `A HARD MESSAGE IN THE MORNING.` · then, large: `SPEAK, LORD, FOR THY SERVANT HEARETH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray those words and listen. Settle, and breathe. If you pray, say Samuel's line once, slowly: Speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth. Then stop talking. Don't fill the silence with requests. Just listen, the way you'd listen in a dark room for someone calling your name. If you don't pray, simply listen: to the room, to your breath, to whatever has been trying to get your attention lately. Nothing may come. That's all right. Samuel ran to the wrong room three times. The bell holds the time.
Speak. The first word of Samuel's answer in the night, and the start of a whole prayer: speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth. Today's word.
Your line: thy servant heareth. Today, in one conversation, listen all the way to the end before you answer. Day three hundred ninety-eight.

screen: `DAY 398 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: SAUL, HEAD AND SHOULDERS TALLER.`

howItsDone: Some Catholics use Samuel's words, speak, Lord, for thy servant heareth, as a short prayer before reading scripture or in quiet adoration, and the chapter is read on a Sunday in Ordinary Time alongside the call of the first disciples.

fork.setup: you're Samuel. God has just told you that Eli's house will be judged. in the morning, Eli asks what you heard. what do you do?
options: tell him everything, and hide nothing.

fork.reveal: Samuel tells him all of it. Eli answers, it is the Lord: let him do what is good in his sight. hearing God can mean carrying a hard word.

original.note: Hebrew: hearing, listening, the root of the Shema. Samuel's line ends with it: thy servant is listening.

trapdoor: what you thought: a sweet bedtime story about a boy hearing voices.
what it means: a boy raised in God's house doesn't yet know God's voice, until an old priest teaches him to ask and to listen. then the word is hard.
what a scholar hears: the Hebrew for heareth shares the root of the Shema. and the text frames the story with a time when the word of the Lord was rare.
